publication.citation: Wang J., Tchapmi L.P., Ravikumar A.P., McGuire M., Bell C.S., Zimmerle D., Savarese S., Brandt A.R. Machine vision for natural gas methane emissions detection using an infrared camera. Applied Energy 257 (2020) 113998

site: Methane Emissions Technology Evaluation Center (METEC), Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado
release_hardware: Metered leak points made from 1/4-inch steel tubing on a separator; flow set by orifice and regulated compressed natural gas
camera: FLIR GF-320 infrared (OGI) camera on a tripod, normal mode (not high-sensitivity); ~15 frames/s, 320x240 grayscale on-camera recording
protocol: Each 24-minute video steps through eight leak-size classes, including class 0, in 3-minute intervals; the authors treat the first 15 s and last 5 s of each interval as not steady
leak_classes_source: Wang et al. 2020, Table 1 (rates with 95% confidence intervals)

MOV_1242.release_location_basis: Inferred: the paper reports 13 pad-1 videos, matching the 13 MOV_12xx/MOV_14xx recordings; the workbook does not name the pad

MOV_1242.segment_timing_basis: Workbook 'Start Time for Leak 0/1 Video Clip' values (0:05, 3:05) read as minutes:seconds, plus the paper's 3-minute interval; unverified interpretation. The executed detector's first alert at about 194 s is consistent with it. Classes after 1 are not labeled in the workbook and are not asserted here.

plant_alignment: Event 1 (MOV_1237): the synthetic plant releases the same metered rates at XV-2104: class 0 (5.3 g/h) before the scenario onset and class 1 (277.7 g/h) from 600 s. Event 2 (MOV_1239) shows a larger metered release than the plant scenario; its rates are not matched. The footage is a different physical scene; only rates are matched where stated.
agent_access: Not an agent tool or frozen evidence: these are facts about the recorded footage, shown to people as the answer key
